title: Sitagliptin
disclaimer: Educational summary of public regulatory and scientific sources (EU product information and assessment reports, clinical trial registers, ESC/EAS guidelines), current as of the Januvia 25/50/100 mg product information published by the EMA on 31 October 2025. This is not medical advice and not promotional material. Treatment decisions must follow the current official product information and a qualified healthcare professional.

blocks.markdown:
## What sitagliptin is

Sitagliptin is a **DPP-4 inhibitor**, a tablet for type 2 diabetes. It helps the body's own **incretin** hormones, which the gut releases after meals to raise insulin, keep working for longer. The dose is one tablet a day, with or without food.

This module is built on the **SmPC** (summary of product characteristics, the regulator-approved reference text for prescribers) for Januvia 25, 50 and 100 mg. Januvia is authorised across the whole EU through the European Medicines Agency (EMA), and Merck Sharp & Dohme B.V. is the marketing authorisation holder. The version used is the product information the EMA published on **31 October 2025**. Where any source disagrees on what is approved, the SmPC wins.

## What it is approved for

For adults with type 2 diabetes, Januvia is approved to improve **glycaemic control**, meaning control of blood sugar, alongside diet and exercise. The SmPC allows it in several combinations:

- On its own, only when metformin (the usual first diabetes tablet) can't be used.
- With metformin.
- With a **sulphonylurea**, a tablet that pushes the pancreas to release insulin, when metformin can't be used.
- With a **thiazolidinedione** (pioglitazone), a tablet that makes the body more sensitive to insulin.
- In three-drug combinations with metformin.
- Added to insulin, with or without metformin.

## What it does to blood sugar

Diabetes trials measure **HbA1c**, a blood test that reflects average blood sugar over the past two to three months. Compared with a **placebo** (a dummy tablet), sitagliptin 100 mg on its own lowered HbA1c by 0.6 percentage points at 18 weeks and 0.8 at 24 weeks, from a starting level of about 8.0%. Added to metformin, it lowered HbA1c by 0.7 points at 24 weeks.

In a direct comparison over 24 weeks, sitagliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.43 points and metformin by 0.57. The EPAR summary concludes that sitagliptin appears slightly less effective than metformin.

For HbA1c, the difference in percentage points is the effect itself. Unlike heart attacks, there are no event rates to express as a relative reduction.

## What it does to the heart

TECOS followed 14,671 people with type 2 diabetes and established heart disease for a median of three years. Heart-related death, heart attack, stroke or hospitalisation for unstable angina occurred in 11.4% on sitagliptin and 11.6% on placebo, a hazard ratio of 0.98 (95% CI 0.89–1.08). Hospitalisation for heart failure was 3.1% in both groups.

TECOS was a **non-inferiority** trial, designed to show the medicine does no harm to the heart. It showed exactly that: no extra harm, and no extra benefit. Lesson 10 explains why that distinction matters.

## What to watch

- Pancreatitis. If it is suspected, stop the medicine. If it is confirmed, never restart it.
- **Hypoglycaemia** (low blood sugar). This is mainly a risk when sitagliptin is combined with a sulphonylurea (4.7–13.8% of patients) or with insulin (9.6%).
- Serious allergic reactions, usually within the first three months.
- **Bullous pemphigoid**, a blistering skin disease.
- Kidney function, which sets the dose.

The only contraindication is allergy to the medicine. Even so, the SmPC says it shouldn't be used in type 1 diabetes, in **diabetic ketoacidosis** (a dangerous build-up of acids caused by lack of insulin), in pregnancy or during breastfeeding.

## What this module is, and isn't

This is a learning module, not prescribing advice. It is refreshed every six months, or straight away if the SmPC changes or a **safety signal** (new evidence suggesting a possible side effect) appears.

One detail to know from the start: the Januvia SmPC gives no revision date of its own, and the leaflet still shows the placeholder '{MM/YYYY}'. So this module is dated by the EMA's publication date instead.

## The gut talks to the pancreas

After a meal, the gut releases two incretin hormones: **GLP-1** (glucagon-like peptide-1) and **GIP** (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide). They signal to the **beta cells**, the cells in the pancreas that make insulin, to release more of it. This only happens when blood sugar is normal or high.

## The enzyme that switches them off

The DPP-4 enzyme breaks these incretin hormones down within minutes. Sitagliptin blocks DPP-4, so more active GLP-1 and GIP stay in the blood.

The result is two effects:

- More insulin is released.
- Less **glucagon** is released. Glucagon is the hormone that tells the liver to release sugar.

Higher insulin and lower glucagon together mean less sugar is made by the liver, and HbA1c falls. The SmPC adds that sitagliptin is highly selective: at treatment doses it doesn't block the closely related enzymes DPP-8 and DPP-9.

## Why it rarely causes low blood sugar on its own

The incretin effect is **glucose-dependent**: it switches off when blood sugar is low. When glucose is low, GLP-1 doesn't stimulate insulin or hold back glucagon. It also doesn't blunt the body's normal glucagon response when sugar drops too far.

Sulphonylureas work differently. They push insulin out even when sugar is already low, which is why hypoglycaemia is a sulphonylurea problem, and becomes a sitagliptin problem only when the two are combined.

## Working alongside metformin

In a two-day study in healthy volunteers, sitagliptin raised active GLP-1, while metformin raised both active and total GLP-1. Together, their effect on active GLP-1 added up. Only sitagliptin raised active GIP.

The SmPC also reports better beta-cell **markers**, measurements taken in the blood that estimate how well these cells are working. Markers show what a medicine does to the body's chemistry. They don't show what it does to the patient's health.

## What happens in the body

Blood levels peak one to four hours after a dose. **Bioavailability**, the share of a dose that reaches the bloodstream, is about 87%, and a high-fat meal makes no difference. Only 38% of the drug binds to blood proteins.

About 79% leaves the body unchanged in the urine, and very little is broken down. The **half-life**, the time it takes for blood levels to fall by half, is about 12.4 hours.

## The kidneys set the dose

Because sitagliptin leaves through the kidneys, its levels rise as kidney function falls. Kidney function is measured as **GFR** (glomerular filtration rate), how much blood the kidneys filter each minute. Exposure is measured as **AUC** (area under the curve), the total amount in the blood over time. Compared with normal kidney function, AUC rises:

- at GFR 60–90 mL/min: about 1.2 times
- at GFR 45–60 mL/min: about 1.6 times
- at GFR 30–45 mL/min: about 2 times
- below 30 mL/min, including dialysis: about 4 times

That's why the dose falls to 50 mg and then 25 mg (Lesson 6). A 3–4 hour haemodialysis session removes only about 13.5% of the drug.

## Few interactions

Only a small share of sitagliptin is processed by liver enzymes, so it has little potential for interactions. Ciclosporin raised sitagliptin's AUC by 29%, which wasn't considered clinically meaningful. Sitagliptin raised digoxin's AUC by 11%, so people at risk of digoxin toxicity should be monitored. Sitagliptin didn't meaningfully change the levels of metformin, glyburide, simvastatin, warfarin or oral contraceptives.

One gap remains: strong inhibitors of the liver enzyme CYP3A4 haven't been studied in people with severe kidney impairment. In those patients, liver breakdown matters more.

questions.stem: Why does sitagliptin on its own rarely cause hypoglycaemia?
options: Its incretin effect is glucose-dependent and switches off when blood sugar is low
questions.explanation: GLP-1 and GIP raise insulin only when glucose is normal or high, and GLP-1 doesn't blunt the glucagon response to low sugar. Sulphonylureas raise insulin regardless of glucose, so combining the two brings hypoglycaemia back.

## The first of its class

Sitagliptin was developed by Merck under the code MK-0431. The US FDA approved it on 16 October 2006, making it the first DPP-4 inhibitor on the market. The US is mentioned here only to anchor the timeline; this module is built on the EU label.

## One approval for the whole EU

Januvia went through the **centralised procedure**, the EU route in which one EMA assessment leads to a single licence valid in every member state. The European Commission granted that licence in March 2007. Merck announced it as the first DPP-4 inhibitor approved by the European Commission.

Because the approval was central, Januvia has an **EPAR** (European public assessment report, the EMA's published evaluation). The original dossier covered nine studies in almost 6,000 patients. It also records that tablets of 25, 50, 100 and 200 mg were developed, but only 25, 50 and 100 mg were authorised.

## What the assessors weren't sure about

The EPAR is candid. For use on its own, sitagliptin was never compared directly with a sulphonylurea. In a trial against glipizide, where both were added to metformin, the two drugs lowered HbA1c similarly. However, the glipizide dose was low: about 40% of patients were on 5 mg a day or less. The assessors wrote that non-inferiority had not been unequivocally proven, and more patients stopped sitagliptin because it wasn't working well enough.

The current SmPC still reports those details, and the EPAR summary says sitagliptin appears slightly less effective than metformin.

## A growing list of combinations

The first licence covered sitagliptin alone and with metformin or pioglitazone. In December 2007 the EU added use with a sulphonylurea, and the three-drug combination of sulphonylurea plus metformin. Later changes brought the licence to the list you'll see in Lesson 4, which includes use with insulin.

## The pancreas question

In March 2013 the EMA began investigating findings that suggested pancreatic risks with incretin-based diabetes medicines, the group that includes DPP-4 inhibitors. The investigation concluded in July 2013.

Today's SmPC carries an explicit warning about acute pancreatitis. In TECOS, confirmed pancreatitis occurred in 0.3% of people on sitagliptin and 0.2% on placebo. The EMA still lists a study of incretin-based therapies and pancreatic cancer among its post-authorisation studies. Lesson 13 follows this thread.

## Children: a negative result written into the label

Under EU rules, the company had to test sitagliptin in children. In a 20-week trial in 10–17-year-olds, HbA1c didn't improve compared with placebo: the difference was −0.2 points, with a 95% CI of −0.7 to 0.3. The SmPC therefore says it shouldn't be used in this age group because it doesn't work well enough.

This is a regulatory system working as intended. A negative trial result was reported openly and changed the label.

## Generics arrive

Generic sitagliptin is now also authorised centrally. Sitagliptin SUN and Sitagliptin Accord, for example, showed that the body absorbs them in the same way as Januvia 100 mg (bioequivalence). The EMA concluded that, as with Januvia, their benefits outweigh their risks.

## One condition behind every use

Every use in the SmPC is for adults with **type 2 diabetes**, a condition in which the body doesn't make enough insulin, or the insulin it makes doesn't work well enough. Each use is also an **adjunct** to diet and exercise, meaning it is added on top of them and never replaces them.

Sitagliptin isn't for type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis, and it isn't for children.

## Use 1: on its own, with a condition

As **monotherapy**, meaning a single medicine with no other diabetes drug, sitagliptin is approved only when diet and exercise haven't been enough *and* metformin can't be used because of contraindications or side effects.

This is why: metformin comes first, and the EPAR notes that sitagliptin appears slightly less effective than metformin when each is used alone.

## Use 2: two medicines together

As **dual therapy**, meaning two diabetes medicines together, sitagliptin can be combined with:

- metformin, when metformin alone isn't enough
- a sulphonylurea, when the highest tolerated sulphonylurea dose isn't enough *and* metformin can't be used
- a PPARγ agonist, meaning a thiazolidinedione such as pioglitazone, when that medicine is appropriate but not enough on its own

## Use 3: three medicines, or insulin

As triple therapy, sitagliptin can be added to metformin plus a sulphonylurea, or to metformin plus a PPARγ agonist, when the two together aren't enough.

It can also be an **add-on** to insulin, meaning added to a treatment already in place: a stable insulin dose, with or without metformin, that isn't giving good enough control.

## Notice what isn't there

Januvia's own indication doesn't name SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists, two newer classes of diabetes medicine. It also makes no claim about reducing heart attacks or strokes. TECOS showed no extra harm to the heart, but it didn't show a benefit either.

The SGLT2 pairing does exist in the EU, but under a different licence: Steglujan, which combines sitagliptin with ertugliflozin in one tablet.

## Where the US label differs

The US indication is broader. It says only that sitagliptin is an adjunct to diet and exercise, with no requirement that metformin be unsuitable. It adds that sitagliptin hasn't been studied in people who have had pancreatitis.

The US label also carries a heart-failure warning. It is based on outcome trials of two other DPP-4 inhibitors, not sitagliptin. The EU SmPC has no such warning. Lesson 10 looks at why.

## The tablets

Januvia comes as round **film-coated tablets** (tablets with a thin outer layer) in three strengths, each with a number printed on one side:

- 25 mg: pink, '221'
- 50 mg: light beige, '112'
- 100 mg: beige, '277'

The **excipients**, the ingredients other than the active substance, include no lactose, and each tablet contains less than 1 mmol of sodium. The tablets keep for two years below 25 °C. Packs range from 14 to 98 tablets, plus hospital-style unit-dose strips of 50.

## One text for the whole EU

The **MAH** (marketing authorisation holder, the company legally responsible for the product) is Merck Sharp & Dohme B.V. in Haarlem, the Netherlands, which also releases the batches. Because the licence is central, every EU country uses the same SmPC, translated into each language.

## Same medicine, other names

The EU has also authorised sitagliptin under other brand names, as a **duplicate marketing authorisation**: a second licence for the same product under another name. According to the Janumet EPAR summary, sitagliptin was authorised as Januvia and Xelevia from 2007, and as Tesavel from 2008. This module hasn't checked whether each duplicate is still marketed.

## Generics

Since its patent expired, generic sitagliptin has also been authorised centrally. Sitagliptin SUN, for example, showed **bioequivalence** with Januvia 100 mg: its blood levels matched closely enough to count as the same medicine. For the 25 mg and 50 mg strengths, the regulators accepted a **biowaiver**, meaning no separate human study was needed because the lower strengths are made in the same way.

## Combination tablets

Two **fixed-dose combinations** (two medicines in one tablet) contain sitagliptin:

- Janumet, also sold as Velmetia: sitagliptin 50 mg with metformin 850 mg or 1,000 mg, taken twice a day. It is for people not controlled on metformin alone, people already taking both medicines separately, or people who also need a sulphonylurea, pioglitazone or insulin.
- Steglujan: ertugliflozin 5 mg or 15 mg with sitagliptin 100 mg, taken once a day, authorised in March 2018. The SGLT2 inhibitor half of the pairing is covered in Lesson 9.

## Outside the EU

The US sells the same three strengths. In 2023 the FDA also approved another sitagliptin product, Zituvio, from Zydus, in 25, 50 and 100 mg strengths. The Swiss label hasn't yet been reviewed for this module.

## The routine

The dose is one 100 mg tablet a day, with or without food. Diet and exercise continue alongside it. The PIL says to take it for as long as the doctor prescribes it, and not to stop without talking to them first.

## Alongside other diabetes medicines

When sitagliptin is added to metformin or pioglitazone, those doses stay the same. When it is added to a sulphonylurea or insulin, the SmPC suggests considering a *lower* dose of that other medicine. Together they can push blood sugar too low.

## A missed dose

The SmPC says to take a missed dose as soon as you remember, but never two doses on the same day. The PIL is more practical: if you only remember when the next dose is due, skip the missed one.

Both say the same thing in different words. It's a useful reminder that the PIL is written for patients.

## The kidneys set the dose

The SmPC asks for kidney function to be checked before starting and periodically after that. The daily dose depends on GFR:

- GFR 45 mL/min or above: 100 mg
- GFR 30 to below 45 mL/min: 50 mg
- GFR below 30 mL/min, including dialysis: 25 mg

On dialysis, the timing of the tablet doesn't matter. The SmPC calls both 45–60 and 30–45 'moderate' kidney impairment, even though only the lower band needs a smaller dose. And when sitagliptin is combined with another diabetes medicine, that medicine's own kidney rules apply too. The lowest threshold across all the medicines decides.

## Liver, age and children

Mild or moderate liver impairment needs no dose change. Severe liver impairment hasn't been studied, so the SmPC asks for caution, although the kidneys do most of the work of clearing sitagliptin.

Age alone needs no adjustment, even though blood levels are about 19% higher in people aged 65–80. Sitagliptin shouldn't be used between 10 and 17 because it didn't work well enough in that age group. It hasn't been studied below age 10.

## Pregnancy, breastfeeding and driving

Sitagliptin shouldn't be used in pregnancy, because there aren't enough human data. It shouldn't be used while breastfeeding either: it isn't known whether it passes into human milk, and in rats it reached levels in milk about four times those in the blood.

Dizziness and drowsiness have been reported, and taking it with a sulphonylurea or insulin can cause low blood sugar. Both are worth keeping in mind before driving.

## Overdose

Single doses of up to 800 mg have been given in trials. They caused only a minimal change in **QTc**, an ECG measure of the heart's electrical recovery time, which wasn't considered clinically relevant.

Treatment of an overdose is supportive, including an ECG. A 3–4 hour haemodialysis session removes only about 13.5% of the drug. Longer dialysis can be considered, and it isn't known whether peritoneal dialysis removes it.
